name: George Smith and the Flood tablet (British Museum K.3375, Tablet XI of the Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh epic)
date: Tablet excavated at Kuyunjik (Nineveh) in the 1850s from the library material of Ashurbanipal, which Hormuzd Rassam dug in the North Palace; identified by Smith at the British Museum in 1872 (exact day not recorded in the sources checked) [uncertain]; announced in Smith's paper 'The Chaldean Account of the Deluge', read to the Society of Biblical Archaeology on 3 December 1872; Daily Telegraph expedition to Nineveh in spring 1873, with the fragment found on 14 May 1873; second expedition November 1873 at the British Museum's expense; book 'The Chaldean Account of Genesis' 1876; third expedition from March 1876; Smith died in Aleppo on 19 August 1876. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist) ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/
creator: George Smith (26 March 1840 to 19 August 1876). At fourteen he was apprenticed to the London firm Bradbury and Evans to learn banknote engraving, taught himself cuneiform, and was taken on at the British Museum to sort and join Kuyunjik fragments. Institutions: British Museum, Society of Biblical Archaeology, and the Daily Telegraph, whose editor Edwin Arnold funded the 1873 dig. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)
form: Physical clay tablet: K.3375, a 7th-century BC Neo-Assyrian cuneiform tablet from Kuyunjik, about 15.2 x 13.3 cm, on display in Room 55 of the British Museum; plus Smith's lecture, journal article and 1876 book presenting his translation. Sources: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_K-3375 ; https://sites.google.com/site/100objectsbritishmuseum/home/flood-tablet
effect_on_arc: The find made Gilgamesh visible to the modern world, but through the wrong door. Smith met the epic first as a flood story, and for decades it was read in the West as a Babylonian parallel to Genesis 6-9 rather than as a poem about friendship, grief and mortality. In 'The Chaldean Account of Genesis' (1876) the hero is 'Izdubar', Enkidu is 'Heabani' and the flood hero is 'Hasisadra'. The name Gilgamesh was only settled in 1890, when Theophilus Pinches published 'Exit Gishtubar!' in The Babylonian and Oriental Record. Smith did see that the flood sat inside a longer narrative, and his 1876 book assembled the first sequence of 'Izdubar' tablets, including the Ishtar episode and Heabani's death, so the arc as a whole began here even if its emotional centre was not yet understood. Sources: https://sacred-texts.com/ane/caog/caog14.htm ; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/60559/60559-h/60559-h.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Pinches ; https://www.wedgepod.org/49-george-smith-the-man-behind-the-headlines-transcript/
critical_response: Immediate public sensation. Gladstone, then Prime Minister, was in the audience on 3 December 1872 and rose to make a speech linking the find to Homer. The Daily Telegraph ran three articles within a week and reported that 'an extraordinary public interest' had been aroused. Smith was recognised as the most gifted reader of cuneiform of his generation, and Queen Victoria granted his widow and children a pension of 150 pounds a year after his death. Later assessments are warm but corrective: Andrew George's critical edition (Oxford, 2003) treats Smith as the founder of Gilgamesh studies, and David Damrosch's 'The Buried Book' (2007) makes Smith's story the frame for the epic's modern life. Sources: https://www.wedgepod.org/49-george-smith-the-man-behind-the-headlines-transcript/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist) ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/
controversies: (1) The undressing story. E. A. Wallis Budge, telling it long afterwards, says the text was crusted with salts and Smith had to wait for the conservator Robert Ready to clean it. When he read the cleaned lines he said 'I am the first man to read that after more than two thousand years of oblivion', rushed about the room and, 'to the astonishment of those present', began to undress. Budge was not a first-hand witness to much of what he reports, and historians warn that some of his information is demonstrably wrong. (2) Religion: the find was read as confirming or undermining Genesis and fed Victorian arguments over biblical criticism. (3) Misattribution: the fragment of 'the greater portion of seventeen lines' that Smith found at Nineveh in May 1873, and presented as filling the gap in the Flood tablet, does not belong to Gilgamesh. It comes from an older flood story, now known as Atrahasis (roughly 1800 BC in origin). Its museum number is often given as DT 42, but no source I checked confirmed the number [uncertain]. (4) Credit: Hormuzd Rassam, who excavated the library, felt his part was played down by the Museum establishment [uncertain]. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/ ; https://www.wedgepod.org/49-george-smith-the-man-behind-the-headlines-transcript/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atra-Hasis
regional_reception: The discovery was a European event: the object went to London, and the scholarship was published in English, French and German. The epic came back to Iraq through Taha Baqir (1912-1984), an Iraqi Assyriologist who published the first Arabic translation made directly from the Akkadian in 1962. It has gone through more than six editions and is still widely read. The Flood tablet itself stays in the British Museum, and I found no formal Iraqi claim for its return [uncertain]. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taha_Baqir ; https://medium.com/@ahmedwindi94/the-clay-reader-b6ec0f6e0e17
method: Traditional cuneiform scholarship and manual physical joining. Smith sorted Kuyunjik fragments by eye, matching script, clay and content, joining pieces and reading the signs directly. He spotted the account of a ship resting on a mountain and a bird sent out, recognised the parallel with Noah, and looked for duplicates among other Nineveh copies to fill the gaps. Part of the text was crusted over, and he had to wait for the museum conservator Robert Ready to clean it. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/ ; https://www.wedgepod.org/episode-49-george-smith-the-man-behind-the-headlines-short-version-transcript/
ai_pipeline_stage: None. The whole process was human: eye, memory and hand. The same Kuyunjik fragments are now being rejoined with computer help by Enrique Jimenez's Electronic Babylonian Library team at LMU Munich, which makes Smith's work the natural 'before' picture. Source: https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/49550/1/Jimenez_New_Fragments_of_Gilgames_and_other_Literary_Texts_from_Kuyunjik.pdf
scale_metrics: The Kuyunjik Collection ('Ashurbanipal Library') is a label for around 32,000 cuneiform tablets and fragments from the British Museum's excavations at Nineveh. Most were gathered on the orders of Ashurbanipal (king of Assyria 669 to about 630 BC), though some are earlier. K.3375 dates to the 7th century BC and measures about 15.2 x 13.3 cm. Smith's 1873 fragment preserved most of seventeen lines and was found in about a week of digging (the fifth day, according to Britannica). He made three trips to the region (1873, November 1873, and 1876) and died on the third, aged 36. I did not confirm the exact line count of Tablet XI or of the Flood episode, so I have left it out. Sources: https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/asbp/whatisthelibrary/ ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/ ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Smith-British-Assyriologist ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)
what_was_found: A Neo-Assyrian copy of Tablet XI of the Standard Babylonian epic. In it Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how the god Ea warned him of the flood the gods planned, how he built a boat and loaded it with his family and animals, how he rode out a seven-day storm, landed on Mount Nisir, and sent out a dove, a swallow and a raven. In the epic this is the story Gilgamesh hears at the end of his search for immortality, just before he fails the sleep test and loses the plant of rejuvenation to the snake. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth ; https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_K-3375
provenance_and_ethics: Excavated at Kuyunjik in the 1850s during the British Museum's Nineveh digs (Rassam in the North Palace) under Ottoman permits, and shipped to London, where it has stayed (registration K.3375, Room 55). That was legal under the rules of the time, but it is part of the colonial-era removal of Mesopotamian heritage to European museums. The digital copy is open: the British Museum collection online, the Ashurbanipal Library Project on Oracc, and the Electronic Babylonian Library all publish images or editions, even though the object stays in London. Sources: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_K-3375 ; https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/asbp/whatisthelibrary/
ai_craft_tension: Smith is the clearest human baseline for the recovery story. What he did by hand is what machines are now asked to do: sort tens of thousands of fragments, spot which belong together, read damaged signs and flag a passage worth attention. What no pipeline would have supplied is the jump he made. He read a line about a ship on a mountain and a bird sent out, knew it was Noah, and knew it would matter to his audience. The later corrections show the limits of a brilliant single reader working fast: 'Izdubar' for Gilgamesh, and a 1873 fragment slotted into the wrong poem. These are the kinds of errors that systematic, machine-assisted matching now catches. The meaning still came from a person, and so did the drama that got a newspaper to pay for a dig.
essay_hooks: A former banknote engraver, self-taught, reads the oldest known flood story in the British Museum and (in Budge's much later and doubtful account) starts undressing from excitement: 'I am the first man to read that after more than two thousand years of oblivion.' The Prime Minister sits in the audience for the lecture on 3 December 1872. A newspaper pays a thousand guineas to send him to Nineveh. On 14 May 1873, about a week into the dig, he pulls out seventeen lines that seem to fill the gap, and they turn out to come from a different, older poem. He calls the hero 'Izdubar' because nobody could yet read the name, and it took until Pinches in 1890 to fix it. He dies in Aleppo in 1876, aged 36. Sources: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/epic-hero-153362976/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Pinches
